title: Episode 184: Richard Nixon: Watergate, the Secret Tapes, and Resignation (1972–1974)

At two-thirty in the morning on June 17, 1972, five men wearing surgical gloves and carrying wiretapping equipment were caught inside the Democratic National Committee headquarters at the Watergate office complex in Washington. What the White House initially brushed off as a 'third-rate burglary' slowly unraveled into the most cataclysmic constitutional crisis in modern American history. Pursued relentlessly by Washington Post reporters Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein guided by the shadowy insider 'Deep Throat,' the investigation exploded when Senate hearings revealed that Nixon had secretly recorded every conversation in the Oval Office. From the fiery 'Saturday Night Massacre' and the mysterious eighteen-and-a-half-minute tape erasure to the unanimous Supreme Court ruling forcing the release of the 'Smoking Gun' tape, Nixon fought an agonizing war of survival before becoming the first and only president in American history to resign from office. Discover the tragic fall of Richard Nixon.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we confront the dramatic, tragic undoing of Richard Nixon. In a span of twenty-four months, the president who had won forty-nine states was brought down by his own secret tape recorders and the cover-up of a botched burglary. Here is George with the story of Watergate, the Saturday Night Massacre, and the final helicopter salute on the South Lawn.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE WATERGATE BREAK-IN: JUNE 17, 1972
In the pre-dawn darkness of June 17, 1972, a twenty-four-year-old night security guard named Frank Wills made a routine patrol of the luxurious Watergate office complex along the Potomac River. Noticing a piece of duct tape placed horizontally across the latch of a basement stairwell door to prevent it from locking, Wills removed it. When he returned an hour later and found that someone had re-taped the door, he immediately telephoned the District of Columbia police. Plainclothes officers arrived and caught five men red-handed inside the sixth-floor headquarters of the Democratic National Committee. The burglars were dressed in business suits, carried surgical gloves, three thousand two hundred dollars in crisp hundred-dollar bills, and sophisticated eavesdropping equipment. One of the arrested men was James McCord, a former CIA officer and the chief security coordinator for Nixon's official campaign organization, the Committee for the Re-Election of the President—satirically known as CREEP. Press Secretary Ron Ziegler dismissed the break-in as a 'third-rate burglary attempt,' while Nixon publicly insisted that no one in the White House was involved. In historical reality, the break-in had been orchestrated by a covert White House unit of political operatives known as the 'Plumbers.' The bizarre arrest inside the Democratic National Committee headquarters set off a chain reaction of investigative reporting that would ultimately shake the foundations of the constitutional republic. The small piece of duct tape removed by Frank Wills revealed a covert world of political espionage that would shatter the imperial presidency forever.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: WOODWARD, BERNSTEIN, AND 'DEEP THROAT'
While most of the Washington press corps ignored the Watergate story as a bizarre, isolated political incident, two young, energetic metro reporters at The Washington Post refused to let it die: twenty-nine-year-old Bob Woodward and twenty-eight-year-old Carl Bernstein. Supported by their courageous executive editor Ben Bradlee and publisher Katharine Graham, Woodward and Bernstein spent months knocking on the doors of terrified campaign workers, tracking the money found on the burglars to a secret slush fund in Mexico and Miami controlled by Nixon's top aides. In dead of night, Woodward met secretly in an underground parking garage in Rosslyn, Virginia, with a mysterious, high-ranking government official code-named 'Deep Throat'—later revealed thirty-three years later to be Mark Felt, the Associate Director of the FBI. Clothed in shadows and smoking cigarettes, Felt guided the young reporters with an unforgettable cryptic mantra: 'Follow the money.' Step by painstaking step, the Post's front-page articles revealed a sprawling, illegal White House campaign of political espionage, wiretapping, tax audits, and dirty tricks directed against political enemies. Woodward and Bernstein's relentless investigation proved that an independent and courageous press is the essential immune system of a free society against the abuse of executive power. Bradlee and Graham's steadfast support of their reporters established a timeless benchmark for journalistic integrity and courageous editorial leadership.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE REVELATION OF THE SECRET TAPES
In the spring of 1973, as public pressure mounted, Nixon accepted the resignations of his top palace guard: Chief of Staff H.R. Haldeman and Domestic Policy Advisor John Ehrlichman, while firing White House Counsel John Dean. In May, the United States Senate convened a special investigative committee under folksy North Carolina Democrat Sam Ervin. Eighty-five percent of American households watched the gavel-to-gavel televised hearings, riveted as John Dean testified under oath that Nixon had been actively involved in the criminal cover-up for months, warning the President that 'there is a cancer on the presidency.' But Dean's testimony was one man's word against the President of the United States. Then, on July 16, 1973, committee counsel Donald Sanders asked a routine question of deputy assistant Alexander Butterfield. Butterfield paused, looked at the cameras, and dropped a constitutional atomic bomb: 'I was hoping you fellows wouldn't ask me that... There is recording equipment in the Oval Office.' Nixon had secretly installed a voice-activated taping system that recorded every single conversation, phone call, and meeting held in the White House since 1971. The sudden revelation of the secret taping system transformed the entire Watergate inquiry, providing an unalterable auditory record of conversations that could not be explained away. Butterfield's revelation showed that technology can preserve the unvarnished truth of history, regardless of attempts to conceal it.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE SATURDAY NIGHT MASSACRE: OCTOBER 1973
The discovery of the secret tapes turned the Watergate scandal into a ferocious legal war over executive privilege. Special Prosecutor Archibald Cox, appointed by the Justice Department to conduct an independent criminal investigation, issued a formal subpoena demanding that Nixon surrender nine key Oval Office tapes. Nixon adamantly refused, arguing that presidential confidentiality was absolute under the Constitution. When Cox rejected an absurd compromise where seventy-two-year-old, hard-of-hearing Mississippi Senator John Stennis would summarize the tapes, Nixon lost his temper. On the evening of Saturday, October 20, 1973, in what became forever known as the 'Saturday Night Massacre,' Nixon ordered Attorney General Elliot Richardson to fire Cox. Richardson refused on principle and resigned on the spot. Nixon then ordered Deputy Attorney General William Ruckelshaus to fire Cox; Ruckelshaus likewise refused and resigned. Finally, Solicitor General Robert Bork, third in the line of succession, complied with Nixon's order and fired Cox. The firing triggered a thunderous explosion of public fury: telegrams flooded Capitol Hill, news commentators discussed a dictatorship, and the House Judiciary Committee began formal proceedings for presidential impeachment. The firing of Archibald Cox provoked a historic constitutional backlash, demonstrating that the American people would not tolerate the weaponization of the Justice Department to shield the President. The public outcry proved that the American citizenry's commitment to the rule of law is the ultimate safeguard against executive overreach.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: 'I AM NOT A CROOK' AND THE 18½-MINUTE GAP
Battered by the public storm, Nixon attempted to regain control of the narrative. On November 17, 1973, fielding questions from four hundred newspaper managing editors at Disney World in Orlando, Florida, a perspiring, defensive Nixon uttered words that became the unintended epitaph of his political career: 'People have got to know whether or not their President is a crook. Well, I'm not a crook. I've earned everything I've got.' But nine days later, when Nixon's lawyers finally surrendered several subpoenaed tapes to Federal Judge John Sirica, another shocking scandal erupted: a crucial conversation between Nixon and Haldeman recorded on June 20, 1972—just three days after the break-in—contained an eighteen-and-a-half-minute gap of loud, buzzing static. Nixon's loyal personal secretary, Rose Mary Woods, claimed she had accidentally erased the tape while answering a telephone call by keeping her foot pressed down on the pedal of the recorder while twisting backwards. But when photographers asked her to demonstrate the 'Rose Mary Stretch,' it became obvious that the contortion was physically impossible. Forensic audio experts confirmed that the erasure was not an accident, but a deliberate, manual re-recording executed multiple times. The suspicious gap on the key recording only deepened public cynicism, turning the White House's legal defense into a subject of nationwide ridicule and disbelief. The physical absurdity of the Rose Mary Stretch only reinforced the public's conviction that the cover-up was reaching its desperate conclusion.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE 'SMOKING GUN' AND THE UNANIMOUS COURT
In July 1974, the crisis reached its legal climax. In the landmark case United States versus Nixon, the Supreme Court ruled unanimously, eight to zero, that executive privilege could not be used to withhold evidence in a criminal proceeding, ordering Nixon to surrender sixty-four additional subpoenaed tapes immediately. Days later, the House Judiciary Committee approved three articles of impeachment against Nixon for obstruction of justice, abuse of power, and contempt of Congress. On August 5, 1974, Nixon's lawyers complied with the Supreme Court order and released the transcript of a tape recorded on June 23, 1972. It was the definitive 'Smoking Gun.' On the recording, Nixon was clearly heard instructing Haldeman to order the CIA to telephone the FBI and tell them to halt their investigation of the Watergate break-in under the false pretext of national security: 'You call them in and say, 'Don't go any further into this case, period!'' The tape proved beyond any shadow of a doubt that Nixon had personally directed a criminal conspiracy to obstruct justice. His remaining political support evaporated overnight. The definitive release of the June 23 tape proved to the entire nation that the cover-up had been directed from the Oval Office itself from the very earliest days. The Supreme Court's unanimous ruling reaffirmed that in the United States, no office or person is immune from judicial scrutiny.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: RESIGNATION AND THE FINAL HELICOPTER SALUTE
On August 7, 1974, a delegation of senior Republican leaders led by Arizona Senator Barry Goldwater walked into the Oval Office. They bluntly informed Nixon that if he faced an impeachment trial in the Senate, he would receive no more than fifteen votes; his conviction and removal from office were absolute certainties. Nixon realized that the fight was over. On the evening of Thursday, August 8, 1974, Nixon addressed the nation from the Oval Office, announcing: 'I shall resign the Presidency effective at noon tomorrow.' The following morning, after a weeping, emotional farewell to his cabinet and White House staff in the East Room, Nixon walked with Pat down the red carpet on the South Lawn to the presidential helicopter, Army One. Reaching the top of the stairs, Nixon turned, forced a tight smile, and thrust both arms in the air in his trademark double-V salute. The helicopter rotors churned, lifting him into the sky. At twelve noon, Gerald R. Ford took the oath of office in the East Room, uttering words that echoed with profound relief across a wounded nation: 'My fellow Americans, our long national nightmare is over.' Nixon's solemn resignation and dramatic departure from the South Lawn reaffirmed the supreme constitutional principle that no man, not even the President, is above the law. Ford's solemn words reminded the world that the American system of constitutional government had weathered the storm and emerged unbroken.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Richard Nixon's resignation marked the end of the greatest constitutional crisis in modern American history, testing the enduring strength of the republic's system of checks and balances. Stepping into the void was an unpretentious, honest Midwesterner who had never sought national office: Gerald R. Ford. Next week, we turn to the presidency of Gerald Ford: the controversial pardon of Richard Nixon, surviving two assassination attempts in seventeen days, the hilarious spoofing by Chevy Chase on Saturday Night Live, and the healing of the American spirit during the 1976 Bicentennial. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
